<reason>A razor-thin win for PRO in an excellent debate. CON built the debate's central architecture — the fork that earlier disclosure is either harmful (worst-case anchors, folded prices for contingent restaurant fees) or useless (cart and payment are both pre-money and seconds apart) — and landed its best blow by turning PRO's anchoring evidence against the remedy. But PRO methodically collapsed the "harmful" horn: itemized cart disclosure preserves itemization (A2.3), and conditional menu policies like "18% for parties of 6+" avoid both worst-case anchors and bundled prices (A4.3). CON retreated from "harmful" to "redundant/rewrite" in Rebuttal 2, yet its closing reasserted harms its own rebuttal had abandoned and claimed costs "never answered" that were answered on the record. Meanwhile PRO's leverage point — firms engineer late revelation precisely because timing changes behavior (A1.5, A4.6) — went unrebutted, undercutting CON's "useless" horn. CON's recalibration dilemma (B4.3-B4.4) was genuinely damaging and PRO never fully explained why the cart differs from payment, which keeps the margin thin. Both sides clipped one turn and both handled the Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formats cleanly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1-B2.2's jiujitsu — "the loss-aversion that makes walking away feel costly at payment operates just as powerfully at the cart," so PRO's own evidence condemns a design the remedy leaves intact — was the sharpest single move and set the fork that structured the rest of the debate. But A4.3's conditional-menu-policy answer escaped the fork's harmful horn, forcing CON to fall back to redundancy, which is why CON's closing harm claims rang hollow.</best_rebuttal>
